html:
1What You Will Learn

Note

Acronyms in this note. LLM: large language model; MCP: Model Context Protocol; SDK: software development kit

  • The parts of an end-to-end architecture: input, processing, output and feedback loops
  • The augmented LLM building block
  • The five workflow patterns and when each fits
  • Agents: when they are justified, and their costs
  • How to select a pattern from the problem's shape

2An End-to-End Architecture

Running case

Lumen Advisory Designs a Claims Intake for a Health Insurer

  • Claims arrive as emails, PDFs and portal forms
  • The system must classify, extract fields, check coverage rules, draft a decision note and let a nurse reviewer approve
  • Every correction by the reviewer should improve the system

Stage Responsibilities Claim-intake example
Input Receive, authenticate, normalize, redact, route Parse PDFs, mask personal identifiers, tag the claim type
Processing Prompts, retrieval, tools, orchestration, model calls Classify, extract, retrieve coverage rules, draft a note
Output Validate shape and content, apply guardrails Schema check, rule check, confidence flag
Action and review Human approval, system updates, notifications Nurse approves; claim system updated
Feedback Logs, corrections, metrics, evals, drift alerts Reviewer edits become eval cases; accuracy dashboard
  • Feedback loops are part of the design, not an afterthought: they feed evaluation sets, prompt changes and monitoring (Modules 11 and 12).
  • Design for failure paths: retries, fallbacks, escalation to a human, dead-letter queue for bad inputs.
  • Keep deterministic code for checks that must always hold (validation, authorization, totals); use the model for language and judgment.
  • Separate concerns: ingestion, orchestration, model access, tools, storage, observability. This supports testing and replacement.
Exam tip

An architecture answer should include validation of model output and a feedback path, not only the model call.

3The Augmented LLM

The augmented LLM is the basic building block: a model enhanced with retrieval, tools and memory. It can generate its own search queries, choose tools and decide what to retain.

  • Tailor the augmentations to the use case and give the model a well-documented interface (tool names, descriptions, schemas).
  • Most solutions are an augmented LLM inside a workflow: the code controls the path, the model does the language and judgment steps.
  • Integration standards such as MCP connect tools and data in a reusable way (Module 8).

4Workflow Patterns

A workflow orchestrates LLMs and tools through predefined code paths.

Pattern How it works Use when Trade-off
Prompt chaining Sequential calls; each uses the previous output; optional gates Task splits cleanly into fixed subtasks More latency, higher accuracy
Routing Classify the input, send to a specialized path or model Distinct categories; accurate classification; easy vs hard queries Misrouting risk; classifier needed
Parallelization: sectioning Independent subtasks run at once Speed; independent aspects Merge logic
Parallelization: voting Same task run several times Higher confidence; guardrail checks Cost multiplies
Orchestrator-workers A central model splits work it cannot predict, delegates, synthesizes Subtasks depend on the input (multi-file changes, research) Cost, coordination
Evaluator-optimizer One model generates, another critiques, loop Clear criteria and measurable improvement from feedback Extra calls; stop rule needed

  • Chaining trades latency for accuracy; routing can send easy queries to a smaller, cheaper model.
  • Sectioning and voting are the two forms of parallelization; voting gives diversity for confidence checks.
  • Use orchestrator-workers only when the subtasks cannot be listed in advance; otherwise plain parallelization is simpler.
  • Evaluator-optimizer needs clear criteria and a maximum number of rounds.

5Agents

An agent is an LLM that dynamically directs its own process and tool use, checks the environment at each step (ground truth) and decides when it is done.

Use an agent when Avoid an agent when
The path cannot be predicted or hardcoded The steps are known
The task is open-ended (research, coding across files) Latency and cost must be low and predictable
You can trust the model's decisions in a sandbox with guardrails Errors would be costly and hard to undo without gates
  • Costs: higher token use and latency, and compounding errors across steps.
  • Controls: stopping conditions (maximum steps), human checkpoints, sandboxes, tool permissions, tracing.
  • Frameworks (the Claude Agent SDK and others) speed up work but add abstraction that hides prompts and complicates debugging. Start with direct API calls, understand the framework's code, and reduce abstraction for production.

6Selecting a Pattern

Problem shape Pattern
One step; good context and examples are enough Single optimized call
Fixed sequence Prompt chaining
Distinct input types Routing
Independent parts; speed Sectioning
Need confidence from diversity Voting
Unpredictable subtasks Orchestrator-workers
Quality improves with critique Evaluator-optimizer
Open-ended path, many tools Agent
Exam tip

"Steps known in advance" means a workflow; "path depends on what is discovered" means an agent. When both could work, pick the simpler.

Exam tip

Validation and a feedback path are part of every end-to-end design; a bare model call is not an architecture.

7Exam Q&A

S1A claims pipeline has five fixed steps, each of which can be validated. Which design is most appropriate?

  • AA single autonomous agent that plans its own steps on each claim
  • BA prompt-chaining workflow with validation gates between the steps
  • COne large prompt that performs all five steps and returns a combined answer
  • DA multi-agent system with one agent per step and a supervisor
Show the answer

Answer: B. Known, checkable steps suit a workflow; it is predictable and debuggable.

S2A support system receives billing, technical and legal questions that need different prompts and tools. Which pattern fits best?

  • ARouting: classify each request and send it to a specialized path
  • BOrchestrator-workers: let a central model invent subtasks for each question
  • CEvaluator-optimizer: generate an answer and critique it until it is perfect
  • DVoting: send each request to several identical paths and take a majority
Show the answer

Answer: A. Distinct categories with accurate classification are the routing use case.

S3An architect wants higher confidence in a content-safety decision. Which approach does that most directly?

  • APrompt chaining: add a second paraphrasing step before the check, so that the content is rewritten twice
  • BSectioning: split the content into parts and check each part once, then publish the combined verdict
  • CVoting: run the check several times or with several prompts and aggregate
  • DRouting: send the content to a smaller model to save cost
Show the answer

Answer: C. Voting runs the check several times or with several prompts and aggregates the diverse outputs, which raises confidence in the decision.

S4A coding task requires editing an unknown number of files depending on the request. Which pattern is most suitable?

  • AA single call with all files pasted into the prompt
  • BRouting to one of three predefined editing templates
  • COrchestrator-workers: a central model decides the subtasks and delegates them
  • DPrompt chaining with a fixed list of file-editing steps defined by the architect in advance for every request
Show the answer

Answer: C. Unpredictable subtasks that depend on the input are the orchestrator-workers case.

S5What is the main risk of choosing an agent for a fixed, well-understood task?

  • AAgents always produce lower quality than workflows
  • BThe agent cannot use tools that a workflow could call, because tools are limited to fixed pipelines
  • CHigher cost, latency and compounding errors without a benefit over a workflow
  • DAgents cannot be monitored with logs and traces
Show the answer

Answer: C. Agents add cost and risk; they pay off only when the path is genuinely unpredictable.

S6Which TWO belong in every end-to-end Claude architecture? Select TWO.

  • AValidation of model output before it triggers actions
  • BA feedback path from corrections and metrics into evaluation and improvement
  • CA single shared credential for all tools
  • DRemoval of all human review to reduce latency
  • EA fully autonomous agent loop with no step limit
Show the answer

Answer: A, B. Validation and feedback are core; autonomy without limits and shared credentials are risks.

S7A team adopts an agent framework and cannot understand why prompts behave strangely in production. What does this illustrate?

  • AFrameworks are never suitable for production Claude systems
  • BPrompts should be hidden from developers for security
  • CThe framework always overrides the model's instructions
  • DFrameworks add abstraction that can hide prompts and responses, so understand the code and reduce abstraction for production
Show the answer

Answer: D. Start simple, understand what the framework does, and reduce abstraction when moving to production.

S8In an evaluator-optimizer loop, which design element prevents endless refinement?

  • AA larger context window for the generator
  • BRunning the generator and evaluator on the same prompt so that they always agree with each other
  • CClear evaluation criteria and a maximum number of rounds
  • DRemoving the evaluator after the first round
Show the answer

Answer: C. Criteria define "good enough" and a round limit bounds cost.

S9A reviewer's corrections on drafted claim notes are not being captured. Which architectural gap is this?

  • AMissing feedback loop from human review into evaluation data and prompt improvement
  • BMissing routing layer in front of the model, so that every review comment is sent to a different model
  • CMissing agent for the review step
  • DMissing parallelization of the drafting step
Show the answer

Answer: A. Feedback loops convert reviewer work into eval cases and improvements.

8Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Stages Input · processing · output validation · review and action · feedback
Augmented LLM Model plus retrieval, tools, memory
Workflows Chaining · routing · sectioning · voting · orchestrator-workers · evaluator-optimizer
Agent Model directs its own path; costs and compounding errors; needs limits and gates
Choose Known steps = workflow; unpredictable = orchestrator-workers or agent; simplest that works
Frameworks Start with direct API calls; reduce abstraction for production
Keep in code Validation, authorization, exact calculation
